formulas.name: Simple interest

variables.name: interest
variables.description: Interest earned or owed, in currency units.

formulas.explanation: With simple interest, you earn the same amount every year because interest is only ever calculated on the original principal. The total interest grows in a straight line with time.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for short-term loans, some bonds and savings where interest is paid out rather than added on.
assumptions: rate and time use the same period

example.story: 2000 is invested at 4 % simple interest per year for 3 years. How much interest is earned?

formulas.name: Total amount with simple interest
formulas.explanation: Adding the simple interest P r t to the principal gives the total amount. Rearranging it answers questions like how long an investment takes to reach a target.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the final balance or the time needed with simple interest.

example.story: How many years does it take 2000 to grow to 2500 at 5 % simple interest?

formulas.name: Compound interest

variables.name: compounding periods per year
variables.description: 12 for monthly, 4 for quarterly, 1 for yearly.

formulas.explanation: With compound interest, interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself. Each period the balance is multiplied by 1 + r/n, and there are n t periods. Over long times this grows much faster than simple interest.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for savings accounts, investments and debts where interest is added to the balance.

example.story: 5000 is saved at 3 % per year compounded monthly for 10 years. What is the final balance?

formulas.name: Continuously compounded interest
formulas.explanation: Compounding more and more often approaches a limit: interest added continuously multiplies the balance by e^(rt). It is the upper bound of what compounding can achieve at a given nominal rate, and it is widely used in finance theory.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it in financial models, option pricing and as a close approximation for very frequent compounding.

example.story: 5000 is invested at 3 % per year compounded continuously for 10 years. What is the final amount?
steps: A ≈ 6749.29, slightly more than with monthly compounding

formulas.name: Effective annual rate

variables.name: effective annual rate
variables.description: The real yearly growth, as a decimal (also called AER or APY).

variables.name: nominal annual rate
variables.description: The quoted yearly rate as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: A rate of 12 % compounded monthly actually grows money by more than 12 % in a year, because each month's interest earns interest. The effective rate is the true yearly growth, which lets you compare offers with different compounding.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare savings accounts, loans and credit cards with different compounding periods.

example.story: A credit card charges 12 % per year compounded monthly. What is the effective annual rate?

formulas.name: Present and future value

variables.name: future value
variables.description: Value at the end of n periods.

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Interest or discount rate per period, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: Money today is worth more than the same amount later, because it can earn interest. Growing a present value forward gives its future value; dividing a future amount by (1 + i)ⁿ discounts it back to today. Solving for P is called discounting.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare payments at different times, value a future sum, or decide how much to invest now for a goal.

example.story: You need 10 000 in 10 years. How much must you invest today at 5 % per year?

formulas.name: Loan or mortgage payment (annuity payment)

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Interest rate per payment period, as a decimal (annual rate / 12 for monthly).

formulas.explanation: A repayment loan is paid off with equal payments that cover the interest and slowly reduce the debt. The payment is chosen so that the present value of all the payments equals the amount borrowed. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones mostly repay the principal.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for mortgages, car loans and student loans with fixed payments.
assumptions: payments at the end of each period

example.story: A 200 000 mortgage at 6 % per year is repaid monthly over 30 years (360 payments at 0.5 %). What is the monthly payment?

formulas.name: Present value of an annuity

variables.name: present value
variables.description: Value today of all the future payments.

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Discount rate per period, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: An annuity is a series of equal payments. Discounting each one back to today and adding them gives a geometric series, which sums to this formula. It tells you how much a stream of payments is worth now, or how big a pension pot is needed for a given income.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to value pensions, lottery payouts, leases or how much you can borrow for a given payment.
assumptions: payments at the end of each period

example.story: A pension should pay 1000 per month for 20 years (240 months). If the pot earns 0.4 % per month, how big must it be at the start?

formulas.name: Future value of an annuity (regular saving)

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Interest rate per period, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: Saving the same amount every period, each deposit grows for a different number of periods. Adding all the grown deposits gives a geometric series whose sum is this formula. It shows how regular small savings add up thanks to compounding.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for savings plans, pension contributions and sinking funds.
assumptions: deposits at the end of each period

example.story: You save 200 at the end of every month for 10 years at 0.4 % per month. How much will you have?

formulas.name: Remaining balance of a loan

variables.name: remaining balance
variables.description: Amount still owed after k payments.

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Interest rate per period, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: The debt grows with interest as if no payments were made, while each payment grows like a savings deposit. The balance is the grown loan minus the grown payments. It shows how slowly a long mortgage is paid down at first.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find how much is left on a mortgage or loan, for example when refinancing or selling a house.

example.story: After 5 years (60 payments) of the 200 000 mortgage at 0.5 % per month with payments of 1199.10, how much is still owed?
steps: B ≈ 186 109, so only about 14 000 has been repaid

formulas.name: Net present value (three years)

variables.name: net present value
variables.description: Today's value of all cash flows; positive means worthwhile.

variables.name: cash flow in year 1
variables.description: Net cash received after one year.

variables.name: discount rate
variables.description: Required return per year, as a decimal.

variables.name: cash flow in year 2
variables.description: Net cash received after two years.

variables.name: cash flow in year 3
variables.description: Net cash received after three years.

formulas.explanation: Net present value discounts every future cash flow back to today and subtracts the initial investment. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the discount rate; a negative one means you would do better elsewhere. The rate that makes NPV zero is the internal rate of return (IRR), which you can find by solving this equation for i.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to decide whether an investment or project is worth doing, and to compare alternatives.
assumptions: cash flows at the end of each year
add more terms for longer projects

example.story: A machine costs 1000 and brings in 400 at the end of each of the next three years. At a discount rate of 8 %, is it worth buying?

formulas.name: Present value of a perpetuity

variables.name: present value
variables.description: Value today of payments that go on forever.

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Discount rate per period, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: A perpetuity pays the same amount forever. Letting n grow without limit in the annuity formula makes (1 + i)⁻ⁿ vanish, leaving M/i. In other words, a capital of M/i earning interest i pays M every period without ever running down.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to value endowments, preferred shares, ground rents and the terminal value in company valuations.

example.story: A scholarship fund must pay 500 every year forever. If it earns 4 % per year, how much must be invested?

formulas.name: Real interest rate (Fisher equation)

variables.name: real rate
variables.description: Growth in purchasing power per year, as a decimal.

variables.name: nominal rate
variables.description: Quoted interest rate per year, as a decimal.

variables.name: inflation rate
variables.description: Yearly rise in prices, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: If your savings grow by 5 % but prices rise by 2 %, your purchasing power grows by less than 5 %. Dividing the growth factor of money by the growth factor of prices gives the real growth. For small rates it is close to nominal minus inflation.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to judge whether savings or investments really keep up with inflation.

example.story: A savings account pays 5 % while inflation is 2 %. What is the real interest rate?

formulas.name: Rule of 72

variables.name: doubling time
variables.description: Approximate number of periods to double.

variables.name: rate in percent
variables.description: Growth rate per period in percent (6 for 6 %).

formulas.explanation: A quick mental shortcut: divide 72 by the percentage growth rate to estimate how long it takes to double. It works because ln 2 ≈ 0.693 and ln(1 + r) ≈ r for small r; 72 is used instead of 69.3 because it is easy to divide and corrects for compounding at typical rates.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for quick estimates of doubling times for investments, debts, inflation or populations.
assumptions: approximation, best for rates of roughly 4 % to 12 %

example.story: Roughly how long does an investment growing at 6 % per year take to double?

formulas.name: Exact doubling time with compound growth

variables.name: rate per period
variables.description: Growth rate per period as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: Doubling means (1 + r)ᵗ = 2. Taking logarithms and solving for t gives this exact formula, which the rule of 72 approximates.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for an exact doubling time with periodic compounding.

example.story: Exactly how long does an investment growing at 6 % per year take to double?

formulas.name: Compound annual growth rate

variables.name: annual growth rate
variables.description: Constant yearly rate that gives the same overall growth, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: Growth over several years is rarely even, but the CAGR is the single steady rate that would turn the starting value into the final value. It is the geometric mean growth rate, not the average of the yearly percentages.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to summarise investment performance, company revenue growth or population growth over several years.

example.story: An investment grew from 10 000 to 16 105.10 over 5 years. What was its compound annual growth rate?

formulas.name: Markup (profit as a percentage of cost)

variables.name: markup
variables.description: Profit as a percentage of the cost price.

variables.name: selling price
variables.description: Price the item is sold for.

formulas.explanation: Markup compares the profit with the cost price. It answers: by what percentage did we raise the price above cost? It is always larger than the profit margin for the same sale, which is a common source of confusion.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when pricing goods from their cost, as shops and wholesalers often do.

example.story: A shop buys a lamp for 80 and sells it for 100. What is the markup?

formulas.name: Profit margin

variables.name: profit margin
variables.description: Profit as a percentage of the selling price.

variables.name: selling price
variables.description: Price the item is sold for.

formulas.explanation: The margin is the share of the selling price that is profit. A 20 % margin means 20 of every 100 in sales is profit. Businesses usually report margins, while markups are used to set prices.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to measure profitability of products or companies.

example.story: A lamp that cost 80 is sold for 100. What is the profit margin?

formulas.name: Adding or removing VAT

variables.name: VAT rate
variables.description: VAT or sales tax rate in percent (for example 20 or 21).

formulas.explanation: Adding VAT multiplies the net price by 1 + v/100. To remove VAT from a gross price, divide by the same multiplier: you cannot just subtract v % of the gross price, because the tax was calculated on the smaller net price.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to add VAT to a quote or to find the price before tax from a receipt.

example.story: An item costs 121 including 21 % VAT. What is the price without VAT?

formulas.name: VAT amount contained in a gross price

variables.name: VAT amount
variables.description: Tax included in the gross price.

formulas.explanation: Out of every 100 + v paid, v is tax. So the VAT inside a gross price is the fraction v/(100 + v) of it: one sixth at 20 %, 21/121 at 21 %.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find how much tax is included in a receipt or to reclaim VAT.

example.story: A receipt shows 121 including 21 % VAT. How much of that is VAT?

formulas.name: Straight-line depreciation

variables.name: residual value
variables.description: Expected value at the end (salvage or scrap value).

variables.name: useful life
variables.description: Years the asset will be used.

formulas.explanation: Straight-line depreciation spreads the loss in value evenly over an asset's useful life. Each year the same amount is written off, so the book value falls in a straight line from the cost to the residual value.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it in accounting for machines, vehicles, computers and buildings.

example.story: A machine costs 50 000, will be used for 9 years and then sold for 5 000. What is the yearly depreciation?

formulas.name: Declining balance depreciation

variables.name: depreciation rate
variables.description: Fraction of value lost each year, as a decimal.

formulas.explanation: With declining balance depreciation the asset loses the same percentage of its remaining value each year, so it loses most value early on, much like a real car. The value decays exponentially and never quite reaches zero.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for vehicles and equipment that lose value fastest when new, and in tax rules that use reducing balance.

example.story: A 30 000 car loses 20 % of its value each year. What is it worth after 4 years?

formulas.name: Break-even point

variables.name: break-even quantity
variables.description: Units to sell so that revenue equals total cost.

variables.name: fixed costs
variables.description: Costs that do not depend on sales (rent, salaries).

variables.name: variable cost per unit
variables.description: Cost of making one more unit.

formulas.explanation: Each unit sold contributes p - v towards paying off the fixed costs. Dividing the fixed costs by this contribution gives how many units must be sold to break even; beyond that every sale makes profit.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it in business plans, pricing decisions and small business projects.
assumptions: constant price and variable cost per unit

example.story: A food stall has fixed costs of 12 000 per year, sells meals at 25 and spends 10 on ingredients per meal. How many meals must it sell to break even?
